episode_title: Financial Crises: Why They Happen, How They Unfold, What to Do

stories.topic: 1929: How a New York Crash Toppled the World
stories.summary: The Fed had already been doing a poor job through the Roaring Twenties when, for reasons still not fully understood, the New York Stock Exchange crashed in 1929. Shocks triggered further shocks until about 30% of the US banking system went bankrupt. Within months the crash was hurting the Indian economy. Ajay draws a direct line from the Great Depression to Adolf Hitler and the Second World War. He adds a twist: FDR and Hitler ran what we would now call Keynesian policies by improvising, not by reading Keynes.
stories.insight: A crash in one market is too small to shake the world by itself. It needs amplification mechanisms to do that. This is why Ajay says financial crises are 'upstream of wars and revolutions', and why 'the fate of the world is on the line'.
stories.quote: How could it be that a stock market crash in New York brought down the whole world? But that's what's interesting. That's the nature of financial crises.

stories.topic: 1991: Anatomy of India's Balance of Payments Crisis
stories.summary: Fiscal deficits ballooned through the late 80s, especially in the political instability after Rajiv Gandhi. That cut domestic savings and raised India's need for foreign capital. Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait then hit remittances. Capital controls meant money could only enter through a few 'patli gallis' (narrow lanes), and these choked. Once everyone was sure the rupee would crash, exporters kept their dollars abroad, importers bought dollars early, and Indians moved assets out of the country.
stories.insight: Once a devaluation looks near-certain, ordinary self-interested decisions all bet on it, and together they make it happen. The lasting lesson is resilience: a country needs many independent channels for capital, not a few narrow ones.
stories.quote: Once everybody believes that the rupee has to depreciate greatly, then every thinking person is trying to bet on that, is trying to speculate on that.

stories.topic: Harshad Mehta and the Delayed Payoff of 1991
stories.summary: In the early 90s, Harshad Mehta extracted money from the banking system and the RBI through a bond and money market scandal. He pumped it into extreme leverage on the Bombay Stock Exchange, which had structural design flaws. The result was a crazy asset bubble and then a crash. This came just as foreign capital was about to flow in after the 1991 reforms. Ajay thinks it delayed the investment boom, which peaked only in 1996-97.
stories.insight: What makes it a financial crisis is the damage to a function of finance, not the losses of particular firms. Prices allocate resources. When they swing wildly, the whole real economy pauses investment.
stories.quote: So I'm not worried about some brokerage firms going bankrupt, some banks getting burned, focus on the functions of finance.

stories.topic: Thailand's Secret Forward Book and the Birth of Macro Hedge Funds
stories.summary: East Asian governments ran fixed exchange rates. When confidence in Thailand cracked, its central bank secretly sold the baht forward on a huge scale to defend it. One day it emerged that the forward position exceeded the entire reserves, and every speculator in the world shorted the baht. A few people who had studied Thailand through macroeconomics saw it coming and made fortunes. Ajay says this is where the 'macro hedge fund' was born. Speculators then took a hard look at Indonesia, South Korea and others, and the crisis spread from country to country.
stories.insight: Bad policy got punished, which keeps policymakers honest. 'Contagion' was just thinking people updating their beliefs, not a disease.
stories.quote: So in a way they had hundred rupees of reserves and they had forward sold hundred and twenty. Okay? And that day all hell broke loose.

stories.summary: George Soros, whom Ajay calls the greatest hero of currency crises, studied the Bank of England's dilemma. Defending the pound would need a sharp rise in interest rates, which would hurt an already weak economy close to an election. So he bet the pound would leave the European exchange rate mechanism and made over a billion dollars in a day. Once a few traders bet against a currency, hundreds more join, because those bets can themselves make the collapse happen. Amit adds that Soros called this 'reflexivity': the world changes through our actions.
stories.insight: A currency crisis is really a macroeconomics problem. Whoever understands the political and economic trade-off a government faces can predict whether it will hold.
stories.quote: So no government can stand up to the combined power of the global financial system, and that is the way it should be.

stories.topic: The UTI / US-64 Crisis of 2000 and a Model Resolution
stories.summary: Around 2000, problems at the Calcutta Stock Exchange, the BSE and UTI's US-64 scheme fed into each other. Ajay admits that Raj Chitale had warned him US-64 would blow up, and that he hadn't understood it deeply. Yashwant Sinha brought Ajay into the Ministry of Finance, where he was 'a humble staffer'. Bimal Jalan and S. Narayan led the response. Sinha heard all the arguments and split the cost 50-50 between public money and the unit holders. When the assets were later sold, the net cost to the government was zero. UTI was privatised, its act was repealed, and the crisis was used to replace the BSE's Badla system with derivatives and a modern clearing corporation.
stories.insight: Good crisis resolution limits moral hazard, gets public money back over time, and uses the crisis to push through overdue reform. It also helps to admit openly where you were wrong.
stories.quote: So the net cost to the government was actually zero. Brilliant, good job on the UTI resolution.

stories.summary: In a 2002 speech, Ben Bernanke was a Fed governor and not yet its chairman. Milton Friedman was on the stage with him. Bernanke told him, about the Great Depression, that the Fed had caused it. Friedman, Anna Schwartz and the young Bernanke had built the body of knowledge on what went wrong in 1929. Six years later, Bernanke ran the Fed through the 2008 crisis and applied it.
stories.insight: Ajay calls this 'how great countries are made': learn from past mistakes across generations, then put the thinkers in the hot seat. Amit adds that it is a rare case of a thinker becoming a doer.
stories.quote: Regarding the Great Depression, you're right. We did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.

stories.summary: The 2008 team was Hank Paulson, an ex-Goldman Sachs man, as Treasury Secretary, and Tim Geithner, a career civil servant, at the New York Fed. Bernanke chaired the Fed, and Larry Summers joined once Obama came in. They let Bear Stearns and Lehman fail but refused to let the functions of finance fail. The Fed's balance sheet grew roughly five-fold, from about $0.9 trillion to $4.5 trillion at its 2014 peak. Inflation stayed under control, and the crisis was largely contained within two or three years, compared with the Great Depression's nearly decade-long slump.
stories.insight: Practical people stop at 10-30% because anything more is unprecedented. Doing whatever it takes requires a theory you trust, in this case one built from studying 1929.
stories.quote: It takes a thinker to say we will do what it takes. And if it takes five X, we'll do five X.

stories.summary: Ajay retells Bernanke's insight about pre-digital America. A local bank manager knew his borrowers personally, down to whether they were upstanding members of the community, and kept their repayment history in paper files. When the bank failed because of loans against shares in New York, that knowledge died with it. The borrower goes to a new bank, run by Vaishnav in Ajay's example, and has to start again with a 10-rupee loan. Multiply this across 30% of US banks and small firms everywhere lose working capital just when they need it most.
stories.insight: Financial intermediation contains a large stock of tacit knowledge. When banks die, that knowledge is destroyed, and that is a separate channel through which crises hurt the real economy.
stories.quote: This history is in your skull. And this history is in your files.

stories.topic: Did Taxpayers Really Bail Out the Fat Cats?
stories.summary: On UTI, Ajay had argued with M. Damodaran, who headed UTI. He now concedes that the temporary fiscal support turned into a big profit once the shares were sold five years later. In the US, TARP, headed by Neel Kashkari, committed about $0.45 trillion. After the assets were sold, a GAO report found the Treasury's loss was only $31 billion. The Fed's crisis-era asset purchases were very profitable, and those profits flow back to the Treasury as dividends. Ajay concludes that, taken as a whole, the US intervention made money.
stories.insight: Judge a bailout on the whole intervention over its full life, not on one leg at one moment. Amit strongly disagrees, arguing that who pays matters even if the totals come out positive.
stories.quote: And I want to put this up loud and clear. Damodaran was right, I was wrong.

stories.topic: It Doesn't Rain, It Pours: India 1997-2001
stories.summary: India was hit by one shock after another. First came the August 1997 Asian crisis. In January 1998 the RBI sharply raised interest rates to defend the rupee. In May 1998 the nuclear tests brought problems from all sides. Then came the Y2K and dot-com bust, and then 9/11. Each blow hurt the real economy, and the real economy had borrowed from the banks.
stories.insight: Banks fail together because they share the same regulator's mistakes and the same business cycle. With 20x leverage, bad times in the economy quickly become bad times in the banks.
stories.quote: So it doesn't rain, it pours, and the Indian economy was punched with one after another of these blows.

stories.topic: IL&FS 2018: A Leveraged Bet on Indian Infrastructure
stories.summary: IL&FS defaulted in 2018. It had some bad internal practices, but its basic problem was that it was a leveraged bet on private-led infrastructure in India, and that bet failed. The crisis then spread to Yes Bank, other NBFCs and real estate developers.
stories.insight: Sometimes a financial crisis is the visible part of a deeper failure in the real economy, here the failure of India's infrastructure model.
stories.quote: So it was a leverage play on Indian infrastructure, and Indian infrastructure did badly.

recommendations.item: The Beauty of Finance (Ep 21 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recommended in the opening. Ajay then reuses its definition of finance to frame this episode.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it foundational to how they think about finance and one of the show's most popular episodes. It is the source of the 'finance is the brain of the economy' framing.

recommendations.reason: Background on Ajay as a participant in financial crises, not just someone who studies them.

recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'a classic episode' that covers Ajay's 2008 role. Ajay says he worked closely with KP Krishnan when Lehman's collapse hit India within hours.
recommendations.reason: An insider account of how India responded to 2008.

recommendations.item: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Ep 67 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited while explaining the East Asian crisis.
recommendations.reason: Explains why the exchange rate is the economy's most important price and why governments managing it invite currency crises.

recommendations.item: What Our Genes and Phones Tell Us (Ep 117 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls 'our EIE episode on alt data' while describing a paper-based 1930s bank with no digital trail on borrowers.
recommendations.reason: Shows how today's data on borrowers, such as phone top-up habits, differs from the bank manager's personal judgement that died with failed banks.

recommendations.item: Who lends to the Indian state?
recommendations.creator: Aneesha Chitgupi, Ajay Shah, Manish K Singh, Susan Thomas & Harsh Vardhan
recommendations.context: Ajay's co-authored paper on India's financial repression, cited in the banking and debt crisis sections.
recommendations.reason: Shows how bank money is forced into government debt, directed credit and politically favoured loans. This makes India's debt look cheaper than it really is.

recommendations.item: SVB, Banking and the State of the Economy (Ep 323 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma, Ajay Shah and Mohit Satyanand
recommendations.context: Suggested right after Ajay's section on banking crises. It was recorded just after the SVB collapse.
recommendations.reason: A deeper treatment of the banking crisis material Ajay covers only briefly here.

recommendations.item: Impossible Germany
recommendations.creator: Wilco
recommendations.context: A mid-episode recommendation prompted by Ajay's talk of the 'Impossible Trinity'. It opens with 'Impossible Germany, unlikely Japan'.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'absolutely magnificent', adding: 'Nothing to do with finance, and thank God for that.'

recommendations.item: Mutual funds with feet of clay
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Shown while explaining securities market crises.
recommendations.reason: Lays out a feedback loop: large corporate bond fund redemptions hit an illiquid bond market, prices and NAVs fall, and that triggers more redemptions.

recommendations.item: Metrics for Intervention (Ep 101 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's framework for state failure in financial regulation.
recommendations.reason: Explains why finance is one of the hardest areas for the state to regulate well.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's 'EIE episode on regulation', cited on why regulators have too much power.
recommendations.reason: Background on why financial regulators will never work perfectly.

recommendations.item: Going Bankrupt in India (Ep 80 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recommended in the 'what can we do' section on resolving failed financial firms.

recommendations.item: The GPT 5 Deep Research Info Dump on Financial Crises
recommendations.creator: ChatGPT
recommendations.context: Linked by Amit in his dissent chapter.
recommendations.reason: He thought it 'pretty good' for historical background and for summarising how Austrians, Keynesians and monetarists, as well as Minsky and Bernanke individually, read each crisis. It helps readers think for themselves.

recommendations.item: Economic Facts and Fallacies
recommendations.creator: Thomas Sowell
recommendations.context: Cited for an alternative history of the Great Depression.
recommendations.reason: Sowell argues the economy began recovering within months of the 1929 crash, and that government intervention then made things worse.

recommendations.item: The Forgotten Man: A New History of the Great Depression
recommendations.creator: Amity Shlaes
recommendations.context: Named alongside Sowell in Amit's dissent.
recommendations.reason: An alternative to the conventional story of the Great Depression; Amit says it is 'worth reading'.

recommendations.item: The Globalisation Episode (Ep 95 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited for its discussion of the Smoot-Hawley tariffs.
recommendations.reason: An example of state intervention deepening the Depression's vicious cycles.

recommendations.item: Economics in One Lesson
recommendations.creator: Henry Hazlitt
recommendations.context: Amit uses Hazlitt's warning to challenge the idea that Depression-era spending, including Hitler's, revived economies.
recommendations.reason: Teaches you to ask not only what government spending appears to do, but what that money would have done if left with consumers.

recommendations.item: Economics in One Lesson (Ep 109 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The episode where Amit and Ajay previously argued about Hitler's spending.
recommendations.reason: Applies Hazlitt's seen-versus-unseen lens to government spending.

recommendations.item: What Really Happened?
recommendations.creator: Lawrence H White
recommendations.context: Amit's main source for seeing 2008 as a crisis of the state, not of capitalism.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a 'great essay' showing how easy money, bad government incentives and quasi-government entities caused the crisis.

recommendations.item: Not What They Had in Mind
recommendations.creator: Arnold Kling
recommendations.context: Cited alongside Larry White on 2008.
recommendations.reason: A whole book making the case that 2008 was a failure of the state.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Suyash Rai on Demonetisation
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Suyash Rai
recommendations.context: Amit invokes Suyash's argument to reject Ajay's claim that the bailouts were profitable.
recommendations.reason: Suyash's point is that a cost-benefit argument fails when one group bears the costs and another gets the benefits.

recommendations.item: In Praise of Floods
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Scott's latest book, used for its flood and forest fire analogies.
recommendations.reason: Shows how suppressing every small disaster builds up a much bigger one. Amit applies this to bailouts and moral hazard.

recommendations.item: The Clash of Economic Ideas
recommendations.creator: Lawrence H White
recommendations.context: Recommended at the end as an overview of competing schools of thought.
recommendations.reason: A good place to start: you see what Keynes, Friedman and others thought, and that 'they were all right in some ways, they were all wrong in some ways.'

core_ideas.concept: A Financial Crisis Is When the Brain of the Economy Breaks
core_ideas.explanation: Finance makes prices, allocates resources and solves people's financing problems: moving money across time, managing risk and funding big projects. A crisis is a sudden, nonlinear breakdown of those functions. One firm failing, or even a whole industry, is not a crisis if the economy can get the same work done through other channels. The hosts care about the functions, not the institutions.
core_ideas.quote: A financial crisis is when there is a sudden and nonlinear impairment of the functions of finance.

core_ideas.concept: Everyone Has Skin in the Game
core_ideas.explanation: Financial crises impose costs on firms and people who did nothing wrong. Ajay's example is a small firm whose IPO plans are wrecked. Both hosts end on the same note: ordinary citizens should learn the basics of how crises work.
core_ideas.quote: So you may not be interested in finance, but the financial system is interested in you.

core_ideas.explanation: Market economies usually correct themselves. Finance, more than any other field, produces loops where bad gets worse. Examples are bank failures worsening the economy, which then causes more bank failures, and falling NAVs triggering redemptions that push NAVs lower still. To understand any crisis, look for the amplification mechanism.
core_ideas.quote: But sometimes in finance particularly more than anywhere else, you end up with feedback loops that if things are bad, they get worse, and because they're worse, they get worse.

core_ideas.concept: The Current Account Deficit Is Investment Minus Savings
core_ideas.explanation: The usual story is that the current account deficit comes from trade. The deeper fact is an accounting identity: a country imports the gap between what it invests and what it saves. Fiscal deficits reduce national savings, so they push up the need for foreign capital. That is how India's late-80s deficits set up the 1991 crisis.
core_ideas.quote: So if you want twenty-five for investment and you only have twenty of savings, you'll import five of capital. It's inexorable. It's an accounting identity.

core_ideas.concept: Avoid a Monoculture: Build Many Pathways
core_ideas.explanation: A resilient financial system has many institutional ways of doing the same job. If banks fail, non-bank finance carries on. For capital flows, India needs twenty big channels free of government involvement, not a few narrow lanes. Design for resilience from the start.
core_ideas.quote: A healthy, successful, resilient financial system is one that has many, many different institutional mechanisms to do the same thing.

core_ideas.concept: Crises Have Scripts, So Learn the Five Types
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's five types are: banking crises; currency crises; debt crises; securities market malfunctions; and mixed crises where several combine, as in Indonesia. Each follows a recognisable script, which lets you see one move ahead, the way a doctor reads a cancer. Practitioners learn the script by living through a crisis. Everyone else should learn it from economic history and books, because 'you don't have to be a hen to know about eggs.'
core_ideas.quote: There's a script in each of them. There's a script of a currency crisis, there's a script of a banking crisis.

core_ideas.concept: Currency Crises Are Macro, and Contagion Is Rational
core_ideas.explanation: Pegging an exchange rate eventually requires painful interest rate hikes. Traders who understand that trade-off can tell when a peg will break, as in Thailand in 1997 and Britain with Soros. Global markets are more powerful than any government, and Ajay thinks that is healthy because it disciplines bad policy. When the crisis spreads to the next country, that is investors updating their beliefs, not an irrational disease.
core_ideas.quote: Governments trying to influence exchange rates are setting themselves up for a lot of trouble.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay borrows the phrase from Merton Miller. Indian banks run about 20x leverage, so a 5% loss wipes them out. Their loans are opaque, with no market price, and illiquid, because there is nowhere to sell them. Bank failures are linked because all banks share the same regulator's mistakes and the same business cycle. Banks also attract political looting, for the same reason robbers target them: that's where the money is. India's saving grace is that banks matter less and less for financing large firms.
core_ideas.quote: Banks are a disaster prone 19th century industry. And they will go wrong because you have too much leverage.

core_ideas.explanation: Friedman and Bernanke identified three Fed failures in the Depression. First, it did not act as lender of last resort, which Bagehot defined as lending freely against good collateral at a penalty rate. Second, it let the money supply contract sharply, causing deflation, which raised the real burden of every debt. Third, as banks died, the knowledge they held about borrowers died too. The remedy is the functional view of finance: let individual firms fail, but protect the functions with whatever it takes.
core_ideas.quote: We have no loyalty to banks, we have no loyalty to NBFCs. Focus on the functions.

core_ideas.concept: Debt Crises: Interest Rate vs Top-Line Growth
core_ideas.explanation: Borrowing from Peter to repay Paul is fine if you are only rolling over principal. Borrowing to pay interest puts you on a treadmill. For a government, the test is whether the nominal interest rate exceeds nominal GDP growth. If it does, debt-to-GDP rises nonlinearly until interest payments crowd out everything else. India hides this through financial repression, forcing the financial system to lend to the government cheaply, which Ajay calls violating the Magna Carta.
core_ideas.quote: If that interest rate is higher than the growth of the top line, then the organization is in a lot of trouble.

core_ideas.concept: Liquid Securities Markets Are the Inner Sanctum
core_ideas.explanation: If finance is at the core of the economy, securities markets are at the core of finance. An illiquid market, like India's corporate bond market, turns a random large sale into falling prices, falling NAVs and more redemptions. The 1990s reformers' answer was deep, liquid markets open to everyone, with clearing corporations that never fail.
core_ideas.quote: The securities markets are the commanding heights of the financial system.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay gives four reasons. First, human cognition: people shaped by twenty good years between ages 20 and 40 forget that things can go wrong, the most leveraged look like heroes, and statisticians fit models only on recent good years. Second, cleverness: finance is a Spy vs Spy game where well-paid, brilliant staff with lopsided payoffs find the gaps in every rule. Third, state failure: public choice problems and too much regulatory power. Fourth, the fallacy of composition: making each bank safe does not make the system safe, because many moves in the same direction add up to an avalanche. Believing perfect regulation can end crises is an illusion of control.
core_ideas.quote: The brain power of Goldman Sachs will always exceed the brain power of the regulators.

core_ideas.concept: The Crisis Toolkit and the Standing Army
core_ideas.explanation: Get the basics right first: regulate each firm properly. Then build a lender of last resort, which India has not yet begun. Then create a financial resolution framework that lets firms fail while protecting small savers. The Financial Resolution Bill that came out of FSLRC stalled after opposition from bank unions. Finally, keep a standing army of experts, data and authority, for example in the Department of Economic Affairs, modelled on America's post-2008 Office of Financial Research. It exists for the crises nobody designed for.
core_ideas.quote: And so we need an unpredictable team of ninjas which will be able to deal with these things as they come along.

core_ideas.concept: Ajay's Heresy: India Should Have a Small Banking System
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says a good banking system is a first-world achievement. It needs privatisation, a resolution law and a strong regulator, which would take India 25 years at best. Until then, he welcomes the steady shrinking of banks' role. India's future, in his view, lies in internationalised securities markets. Amit warns that this sounds like central planning: 'don't use state coercion to get there.'
core_ideas.quote: A healthy sophisticated India is a deeply internationalized securities markets based financial system. If it becomes a banking based financial system, you're just asking for trouble.

core_ideas.explanation: Pure laissez-faire has a messy history. Only state-backed money with inflation targeting has worked well, and the world worked out inflation targeting only in 1987, in New Zealand. Crypto may mature but is still chaotic. The populist claim that bailouts protect fat cats ignores what the data show over time. Indian-style central planning ('ban it') suffocates innovation. Ajay's middle path is to let sophisticated finance grow, implement FSLRC, and accept that crises will come.
core_ideas.quote: The market economy is not a tidy, centrally planned company town. The market economy is an unpredictable bubbling of the human heart, figuring out new things all the time.

core_ideas.explanation: In the Austrian view, crises begin with easy credit from central banks: the Roaring Twenties, and Alan Greenspan's long run of cheap money. State intervention then deepens them. Amit cites the Smoot-Hawley tariffs, the Community Reinvestment Act pushing banks to lend to people who weren't creditworthy, Fannie and Freddie, and rating agency incentives. He reads Bernanke's apology as the Fed admitting state failure. He also disputes the claim that Hitler's spending revived Germany, saying the recovery began before Hitler came to power.
core_ideas.quote: When I think about 2008, to me it was a failure of the state.

core_ideas.concept: Moral Hazard and Who Really Pays
core_ideas.explanation: Bailouts teach firms they will be rescued, which encourages reckless risk-taking and privatises profits while socialising losses. Amit rejects the argument that the bailouts made money later. He uses Suyash Rai's test: a cost-benefit argument fails when one group bears the cost and another gets the benefit. Bailouts are funded by everyone's taxes, including the indirect taxes paid by the poorest.
core_ideas.quote: The taxes of the beggar at the traffic signal who pays a GST when she buys salt and soap.

core_ideas.concept: In Praise of Floods: Small Failures Prevent Big Ones
core_ideas.explanation: Amit draws on James C. Scott. Dams and embankments raise a river above the surrounding land until the eventual flood is far worse. Putting out every small forest fire builds up fuel for a fire the size of a state. In the same way, suppressing every small financial failure may store up a bigger crisis. The Austrian response to systemic risk is 'so be it'. Otherwise you are just kicking the can down the road.
core_ideas.quote: So by trying with your hubris to solve a small problem and getting in the way of nature and the flow of water and the spread of fire, by being too much a man of system about that, you have actually created a greater problem down the road.

core_ideas.concept: Be Sceptical, Not Dismissive, of Convention
core_ideas.explanation: Amit places Ajay's view slightly to the right of mainstream economics. He reminds listeners that conventional wisdom keeps changing, as accounts of the Great Depression have. Read the Austrians, Keynesians and monetarists, and keep studying economic history.
core_ideas.quote: So we should always by default be sceptical of convention, not dismissive of it, but sceptical of convention and keep informing ourselves on economic history and what great thinkers everywhere have to say.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit says he is really a 'gentle listener' learning from Ajay, then adds: 'If you don't agree, why are you a regular viewer? It's because of me, isn't it? I'm so hot.'

Explaining what a neighbourhood bank manager knows about a regular borrower, Ajay describes himself: 'when I get drunk in the evening, I'm extremely temperate in my ways. I only have milk in a bar. Okay, I'm that kind of guy.'

Amit's 'Incredible Trinity': he owes Vaishnav 100, Vaishnav owes Namsita 100, Namsita owes Amit 100. He borrows 100 from Ajay and everyone settles up, so total debt falls from 300 to 100, 'and it's actually zero because I'm not gonna fucking pay you back.' Ajay earnestly turns it into a lesson on network effects in crises, then explains: 'I am a one-track mind... when I do finance, I do it seriously.' Amit: 'You've just dissected a frog, but well done.'

Ajay on who makes a deep, liquid market: 'There should be foreigners, there should be Indians, there should be Bengalis, there should be Tamilians, there should be algorithmic traders, there should be astrology traders.'

Ajay on complacent practitioners who think execution is all that matters and that 'watching these verbose males on long-winded shows is completely a waste of time'. Earlier he lists among humanity's failings: 'People fail to watch an EIE episode on financial crisis.'
Ajay on the 'lefties' who say evil capitalists profited from Thailand's collapse: 'No, it's called capitalism. This is how it works.'

Ajay, defending his small-banking dream: 'So I said I hate to pick winners, I hate to pick losers. But I am proposing a loser.' Amit: 'I mean you're free to imagine your dream world, but don't use state coercion to get there.'

After Ajay rejects the 'fat cat' story, Amit starts a pun: 'So Ajay, what do you call the confession of a cat?' Ajay deflects: 'The wordsmithing that is required is what do you call the confession of a fat cat, and we need to find a correct answer. I want to tell you about financial crisis.' Amit: 'No fooling around. Continue.'

Spy vs Spy: 'you have to be my age to know something called Mad Magazine and a cartoon strip called Spy versus Spy,' says Ajay, to describe the cat-and-mouse game between regulators and bankers. Amit: 'Are you thirteen again? Spy versus spy was amazing.'
The bank robber's line, 'Why do you rob banks? Answer, because that's where the money is.' Ajay uses it to explain why every political economy tries to grab bank money.
Ajay's twist on the old adage: 'Those who fail to learn from history are doomed to participate in its repetition.'
Ajay opens by noting that we pay attention to aviation safety only when 'an Air India plane crashes into a medical college hostel in Amdavad'. Financial crises get the same limited attention span.
Walter Bagehot's lender-of-last-resort rule, in Ajay's words: 'Lend freely against good collateral at a penal rate. So people should cry when they come asking for credit from a central bank.'

Ajay treats the flawed pre-2008 securitisation models as a scientific gap, not a moral failure: 'You needed to figure out the photoelectric effect in order to play correctly around it.' He credits 'our friend' Viral Acharya with improving understanding of those products.
The East Asian crisis, says Ajay, 'is where the word macro hedge fund was born', because a few people analysed Thailand through macroeconomics and saw the peg would break.

New Zealand, 1987: Ajay says only then did central banking 'get to the basics' with inflation targeting. 'Conventional money took a thousand years before we got to inflation targeting', which is why he is patient but sceptical about crypto.
Magna Carta: describing India's financial repression, Ajay says 'We basically violate the Magna Carta,' because the state forcibly takes money from the economy to fund its debt.
Hyman Minsky: Amit names him and Ben Bernanke as two of Ajay's great influences on financial crises. The ChatGPT deep research report in the show notes summarises what each would think.
